title: Artemis, our clinical trial results are published in Pediatric Researc
summary: ARTEMIS is published in Pediatric Research, a peer reviewed Nature Portfolio journal. Randomized, double blind, placebo controlled. Three findings: it was safe and well tolerated, our Bifidobacterium strains colonized and got to work, and they stick around. Most probiotics are visitors. Ours move in.
body_markdown:
**ARTEMIS is published in *Pediatric Research* , a peer reviewed Nature Portfolio journal. Randomized, double blind, placebo controlled. And we couldn't be more excited about the results.**


Two years ago, we set out to answer a question no one had properly answered in this country: what does the gut of a modern American baby actually look like?


We ran the My Baby Biome study, the largest study ever conducted in the U.S. to map the infant gut microbiome. 412 babies. 48 states. And the answer we got back surprised us.


90% of U.S. babies are missing one or more keystone strains of


Bifidobacterium


, the group of bacteria that should dominate a healthy infant gut.


Then we went looking for something that would put them back, and found that nothing did. Most probiotics available to parents were built on strains from decades ago and aren’t paired with the prebiotics they actually use. Close enough to sound right on a label. Not close enough to restore what these babies were missing.


So we made it ourselves. A synbiotic built to deliver the exact microbes modern babies lack, paired with the exact food those microbes need to survive.


Then we did the thing almost no one in this category does. We put it through a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.


Those results were published in


Pediatric Research


, a peer-reviewed Nature Portfolio journal. The trial is called ARTEMIS, and is the largest U.S. clinical study of an infant synbiotic.


Here's what it found, and what it means for your child.


**Why Bifidobacterium is the group that matters**


Bifidobacterium


is the bacteria a baby's gut is built around: it digests the sugars in breast milk, keeps harmful bacteria from settling in, and helps train a brand new immune system. In a healthy baby, it doesn't just live there. It runs the place.


**What our clinical trial did**


ARTEMIS enrolled 114 infants and toddlers: 58 infants aged 2 to 12 months, and 56 toddlers aged 12 to 24 months.


Half received our synbiotic. Half received a placebo, identical in appearance and texture. Neither the families nor our scientists knew who received which until the study closed.


That design is the reason this trial counts. Randomization removes selection bias. Blinding removes wishful thinking, which is not a small force when a parent desperately wants something to work. A placebo arm tells you what would have happened anyway. Strip those away and you have testimonials, which is what most of this category runs on.


Children took it daily for four weeks. Then they stopped, and we kept measuring for two more. We sampled at four separate timepoints.


**Finding 1: It was safe and well tolerated**


Babies taking our synbiotic experienced no more gas or fussiness than babies on placebo. We assessed this with a validated tolerability scale built specifically for infants and toddlers, and we asked repeatedly throughout rather than once at the end. No serious safety concerns were tied to the product.


Here is why that finding matters. Babies are gassy. That is a fact of infancy, not a product defect, and any company that promises to eliminate it is selling you something. What we needed to demonstrate is that adding a daily supplement to your child's routine doesn't make things worse.


And it didn't.


**Finding 2: Our strains colonized, and got to work**


This is where the trial gets genuinely interesting.


Our hero strain,


B. infantis


, increased significantly in both infants and toddlers. That's the species this entire product was designed around.


But detection alone is a weak result. A bacterium can be present and metabolically idle. The harder question is whether it's doing anything.


It was. Alongside the bacteria, we saw a rise in the genes gut microbes use to digest HMOs. The metabolic machinery scaled up in step with the population, which is precisely the mechanism the formulation was designed to produce.


And the community around our strains shifted too. Colonization was associated with measurable changes in the composition and metabolic pathways of the wider microbiome. Our strains weren't occupying space. They were changing the ecosystem they had joined.


That distinction is the whole point, and it's worth stating plainly:


showing up shows the supplement survived the trip. Changing the ecosystem shows it's working.


**Finding 3: They stick around**


Most probiotics are visitors. Ours move in.


Most products pass straight through and never colonize. In our trial, ours did.


Two reasons. First, the strains: we found ours in healthy modern babies, so they can compete in the gut your child actually has. Second, we feed them. Bacteria with nothing to eat don't stay.


The right strains, and the food that keeps them. That's the difference between one strain passing through and another taking hold.


**And one finding we're still chasing**


Toddlers taking our synbiotic showed a statistically significant improvement in sleep quality compared with placebo.


We're telling you because it's in the paper. We're also going to tell you precisely what it does and doesn't mean, because this is exactly the kind of result the supplement industry oversells.


We tracked sleep as part of tolerability. Gut discomfort is one of the most common reasons small children wake at night, so sleep was one way we assessed whether the product was gentle. The signal appeared in toddlers, not infants. It came from caregiver questionnaires, not a validated sleep instrument. The study was never designed to evaluate sleep rigorously, and we say so in the paper.


So we are not going to tell you this helps your child sleep. We haven't earned that claim.


What we're going to do is design a study that can actually answer it. If a more comfortable gut means more sleep for a two-year-old, that is worth understanding properly, and worth proving before anyone prints it on a label.


We'd rather tell you what we don't know yet than sell you something we haven't demonstrated.


**Why we put ourselves through this**


Walk any pharmacy aisle and you'll find a wall of infant probiotics. Nearly every one will tell you it works.


Very few have been through a randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Many are built on strains isolated decades ago. Most deliver bacteria without the food they actually eat.


We don't think that's an acceptable standard for something you give a six-month-old every morning.


ARTEMIS is our third peer-reviewed publication, following work in


Cell Host & Microbe


and


Communications Biology


. Together with My Baby Biome, it forms one of the most extensively published clinical research programs on infant synbiotics and the developing infant microbiome in the United States.


We're not telling you that to impress you. We're telling you because the bar in this category is low, and we intend to raise it. You should not have to take anyone's word for this, ours least of all.


You should be able to read the study. It's open access.


[Read the full paper in Pediatric Research →](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41390-026-05318-4)


Jarman JB, Torres PJ, Baum C, Tinoco J, Sato H, Soares Rasteiro C, Selbrede R, Insel R, Culler SJ, Van Dien S. Safety, tolerability, and gastrointestinal effect of a Bifidobacterium-based synergistic synbiotic in infants and toddlers. Pediatric Research (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41390-026-05318-4. ARTEMIS trial, NCT06746285.
